concepts.title: Uniform convergence
concepts.summary: One $N$ that works for every $x$ at once: $\sup|f_n-f|\to0$.

blocks.title: Uniform convergence
blocks.md:
Pointwise convergence (lesson 8.8) lets each point converge at its own speed. This lesson asks for one speed that works everywhere at once.

**In this lesson you will learn to:**
- state the definition of uniform convergence and see how it differs from pointwise convergence
- test for it by computing the **sup distance** $\sup_{x\in E}|f_n(x)-f(x)|$
- prove that convergence is **not** uniform by finding witness points
- use the uniform Cauchy criterion and the **Weierstrass M-test** for series of functions

**You need:** pointwise convergence (8.8), the supremum $\sup$ (2.9), the $\varepsilon$–$N$ definition of convergence (3.4), the order of quantifiers (1.3), and convergence of series (4.3).

## The problem with pointwise convergence

Recall from lesson 8.8 that $f_n(x)=x^n$ converges pointwise to $0$ on $[0,1)$: at each fixed $x<1$, the numbers $x^n$ shrink to $0$.

Now fix a target, say $\varepsilon=\tfrac12$, and ask at each point: from which $n$ on is $x^n<\tfrac12$?

- At $x=0.9$: $0.9^6\approx0.53$ but $0.9^7\approx0.48$, so you need $n\ge7$.
- At $x=0.99$: you need $n\ge69$.
- At $x=0.999$: you need $n\ge693$.

The closer $x$ is to $1$, the longer you wait. Every point gets there eventually, but there is **no single $N$** that works for all $x\in[0,1)$ at once. Whatever $N$ you pick, some $x$ close to $1$ still has $x^N\ge\tfrac12$.

This matters in practice. In lesson 8.8 you saw that pointwise limits can lose continuity and that integrals of $f_n$ need not converge to the integral of the limit. The cure for both, as the next two lessons show, is to insist on one $N$ that serves every $x$. That is uniform convergence.

blocks.title: Converging everywhere is not converging uniformly
blocks.md:
"$f_n(x)\to f(x)$ at every point $x$" only says that each point has its **own** $N(x)$. It does not say the numbers $N(x)$ stay bounded.

For $x^n$ on $[0,1)$ they don't: $N(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to1$. There is no largest one to take, because there are infinitely many points and the values grow without limit.

blocks.question: A student argues: "For each $x\in[0,1)$ there is an $N(x)$ with $x^n<\tfrac12$ for $n\ge N(x)$. So take $N$ to be the largest of the $N(x)$, and it works for every $x$." What is wrong?
options: Nothing: this proves the convergence is uniform
There are infinitely many $N(x)$ and they grow without bound as $x\to1$, so there is no largest one
$N(x)$ does not exist for $x$ close to $1$
The largest $N(x)$ exists but is not an integer
blocks.explanation: Taking the largest works for finitely many points, not infinitely many. Here $N(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to1$ (e.g. $7$, $69$, $693$, …), so the set of $N(x)$ is unbounded and has no maximum. Each $N(x)$ does exist, since $x^n\to0$ at each point, and integers are not the issue.

blocks.md:
## The definition

**Plain words.** Draw the graph of the limit $f$ and a band of half-width $\varepsilon$ around it, from $f-\varepsilon$ up to $f+\varepsilon$. The sequence converges **uniformly** if, however thin the band, from some $N$ on the **whole** graph of every $f_n$ lies inside it.

**Definition.** Let $f_n,f:E\to\mathbb{R}$. Then $f_n\to f$ **uniformly on $E$** if

$$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N\ \forall x\in E:\ |f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon.$$

Compare pointwise convergence: $\forall x\ \forall\varepsilon\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N$. The only change is that "$\forall x$" has moved **after** "$\exists N$". So $N$ is chosen knowing only $\varepsilon$, and must then work for every $x$. As in lesson 1.3, moving a $\forall$ past an $\exists$ makes the statement stronger.

**Examples.**
- $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{n}$ on $[0,1]$. For every $x$, $|x/n|\le\frac1n$. Given $\varepsilon$, take $N>\frac1\varepsilon$; then $|f_n(x)|\le\frac1n<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$ and **all** $x$. Uniform.
- $f_n(x)=\dfrac{\sin(nx)}{n}$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$. Since $|\sin|\le1$, $|f_n(x)|\le\frac1n$ for every real $x$. Uniform, even though the domain is unbounded.
- **Edge case:** $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{n}$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$. At each $x$ it tends to $0$, but at $x=n$ we have $f_n(n)=1$. So no $N$ works for every $x$: pointwise but **not** uniform. The same formula can be uniform on one set and not on another.

**Non-example.** $x^n$ on $[0,1)$, as above.

blocks.question: Let $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{n}$ on $[0,5]$ and $\varepsilon=0.01$. Which $N$ makes $|f_n(x)|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$ and all $x\in[0,5]$ at once?
options: No single $N$ exists, because $N$ depends on $x$
blocks.explanation: The worst point is $x=5$, where $|f_n(5)|=\frac5n$. We need $\frac5n<0.01$, i.e. $n>500$, so $N=501$ works for every $x$. $N=100$ gives $\frac{5}{100}=0.05$ at $x=5$, too big; $N=10$ is worse. A single $N$ does exist here, because the bound $\frac5n$ does not depend on $x$.

blocks.md:
## The sup distance

Checking "for every $x$" directly is awkward. It is easier to measure the **worst gap** between $f_n$ and $f$ over the whole set:

$$M_n=\sup_{x\in E}|f_n(x)-f(x)|.$$

(Recall from lesson 2.9: $\sup$ is the least upper bound, which exists even when no largest value is reached.) $M_n$ is also written $\|f_n-f\|_\infty$, read "the sup norm of $f_n-f$".

**Theorem.** $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$ if and only if $M_n\to0$.

Why: if $M_n<\varepsilon$, then every gap $|f_n(x)-f(x)|$ is at most $M_n<\varepsilon$. Conversely, if every gap is below $\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$, then $M_n\le\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$. (Note "$\le$", not "$<$": a supremum of numbers below $\varepsilon$ can equal $\varepsilon$. That is harmless, since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary.)

**Examples.**
- $x^n$ on $[0,a]$ with $0\le a<1$: $x^n$ increases with $x$, so $M_n=a^n\to0$. Uniform.
- $x^n$ on $[0,1)$: $M_n=1$ for every $n$. The value $1$ is never reached, since $x^n<1$ on $[0,1)$, but it is the least upper bound. Not uniform.
- $\dfrac{x}{1+nx^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$: calculus gives the maximum at $x=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt n}$, so $M_n=\frac{1}{2\sqrt n}\to0$. Uniform.

**Two facts to remember.** Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, since each gap is at most $M_n$. So the only possible uniform limit is the pointwise limit: always find $f$ first, then compute $M_n$.

blocks.title: Testing a sequence for uniform convergence

blocks.question: Does $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+nx^2}$ converge uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: No, the supremum of $|f_n|$ is $1$ for every $n$
No, it does not even converge pointwise
Yes, but only on bounded intervals
blocks.explanation: The pointwise limit is $0$. By calculus, $|f_n|$ is maximised at $x=\pm1/\sqrt n$, where $|f_n|=\frac{1}{2\sqrt n}\to0$. So the convergence is uniform on all of $\mathbb{R}$, not just on bounded intervals. The sup is not $1$: for example $|f_1(x)|\le\frac12$ everywhere.

blocks.md:
## Showing convergence is not uniform

To prove convergence is **not** uniform, negate the definition (the rules are in lesson 1.3):

$$\exists\varepsilon_0>0\ \forall N\ \exists n\ge N\ \exists x\in E:\ |f_n(x)-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon_0.$$

In practice: find a fixed $\varepsilon_0$ and, for each $n$, a **witness point** $x_n$ where the gap is still at least $\varepsilon_0$. Then $M_n\ge\varepsilon_0$ for every $n$, so $M_n\not\to0$. The witness usually moves with $n$, chasing the trouble spot.

**Examples.**
- $x^n$ on $[0,1)$: take $x_n=2^{-1/n}$, which lies in $[0,1)$. Then $x_n^n=\tfrac12$, so the gap is $\tfrac12$ for every $n$. Here $\varepsilon_0=\tfrac12$.
- $nxe^{-nx}$ on $[0,1]$: the pointwise limit is $0$, and at $x_n=\frac1n$ the value is $e^{-1}=\frac1e$ for every $n$. So $\varepsilon_0=\frac1e$ works.

**Edge case.** A **fixed** point is never a witness. At any single $x$ the gap tends to $0$, because the sequence converges pointwise. The witnesses must move with $n$.

**Uniform on pieces.** $x^n$ converges uniformly on $[0,a]$ for every $a<1$, yet not on $[0,1)$, which is the union of all these intervals. Uniform convergence on two sets $A$ and $B$ does give uniform convergence on $A\cup B$ (the sup over $A\cup B$ is the larger of the two sups). It can fail for infinitely many sets.

blocks.title: Worked example: $x^n$ on $[0,a]$ versus $[0,1)$
blocks.problem: Show that $f_n(x)=x^n$ converges to $0$ uniformly on $[0,a]$ for each fixed $a<1$, but not uniformly on $[0,1)$.
blocks.solution:
**On $[0,a]$.** $x^n$ is increasing in $x$, so $\sup_{[0,a]}|x^n-0|=a^n\to0$ since $0\le a<1$. Hence the convergence is uniform.

**On $[0,1)$.** The pointwise limit is $0$, and

$$\sup_{x\in[0,1)}|x^n-0|=1\quad\text{for every }n,$$

since $x^n\to1$ as $x\to1^-$. So $M_n\not\to0$. Concretely, with $\varepsilon_0=\frac12$ and $x_n=2^{-1/n}\in[0,1)$ we have $x_n^n=\frac12$, so no single $N$ works. $\blacksquare$

The moral: the convergence is uniform on every closed interval $[0,a]$ that stays away from $1$, and fails only because of points near $1$.

blocks.question: You want to show that $f_n(x)=nxe^{-nx}$ does not converge uniformly to $0$ on $[0,1]$. Which choice of points does the job?
blocks.explanation: At $x_n=\frac1n$, $f_n(x_n)=1\cdot e^{-1}=\frac1e$ for every $n$, so the gap never drops below $\frac1e$. At $x=1$ the value is $ne^{-n}\to0$, and at $x=0$ it is $0$: fixed points never work, since the sequence converges at each point. At $\frac1{n^2}$ the value is $\frac1ne^{-1/n}\to0$, so that witness moves too fast.

blocks.md:
## Series of functions: the Cauchy criterion and the M-test

Many functions are defined as series, like $\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$, whose sum has no simpler formula. A series of functions $\sum g_k$ **converges uniformly** on $E$ if its partial sums $S_n(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n g_k(x)$ converge uniformly. But how do you compute $M_n$ when you don't know the limit?

**Uniform Cauchy criterion.** Just as for sequences of numbers (lesson 3.12), you can avoid the limit: $(f_n)$ converges uniformly on $E$ if and only if

$$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall m,n\ge N:\ \sup_{x\in E}|f_n(x)-f_m(x)|<\varepsilon.$$

**Weierstrass M-test.** Suppose there are numbers $M_k$, **not depending on $x$**, with

$$|g_k(x)|\le M_k\ \text{ for all } x\in E,\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_k M_k<\infty.$$

Then $\sum g_k$ converges uniformly (and absolutely) on $E$. In words: dominate each term by a constant, and check the constants form a convergent series.

**Examples.**
- $\sum\frac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$: $|\sin(kx)/k^2|\le\frac1{k^2}$ and $\sum\frac1{k^2}<\infty$. Uniform on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
- $\sum\frac{x^k}{k^2}$ on $[-1,1]$: $|x^k/k^2|\le\frac1{k^2}$. Uniform.
- **Edge case:** for $\frac{x^k}{k^2}$, $M_k=\frac1k$ is also a valid bound, but $\sum\frac1k$ diverges, so with that choice the test says nothing. Choose the bounds well.

**Non-example.** $\sum x^k$ on $(-1,1)$: the best bound is $\sup|x^k|=1$, and $\sum1$ diverges. Indeed the series is not uniformly convergent there: its tail $\sum_{k>n}x^k=\frac{x^{n+1}}{1-x}$ is unbounded near $x=1$.

steps.title: Set up
steps.md: Suppose $|g_k(x)|\le M_k$ for all $x\in E$, and $\sum M_k<\infty$. Let $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n g_k$. We will show $(S_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy.

steps.title: Estimate the gap between partial sums
steps.md:
For $m>n$ and every $x\in E$, by the triangle inequality,

$$|S_m(x)-S_n(x)|=\Big|\sum_{k=n+1}^m g_k(x)\Big|\le\sum_{k=n+1}^m|g_k(x)|\le\sum_{k=n+1}^m M_k.$$

The right side does **not** involve $x$. This is exactly why the $M_k$ must be constants.

steps.title: Use the convergence of $\sum M_k$
steps.md: The partial sums of $\sum M_k$ converge, so they are Cauchy (lesson 3.12). Given $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $\sum_{k=n+1}^m M_k<\varepsilon$ whenever $m>n\ge N$.

steps.title: Take the sup over $x$
steps.md: Since the bound holds for every $x$, $\sup_{x\in E}|S_m(x)-S_n(x)|\le\sum_{k=n+1}^m M_k<\varepsilon$ for $m>n\ge N$. So the partial sums are uniformly Cauchy.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.md: By the uniform Cauchy criterion, $\sum g_k$ converges uniformly on $E$. Applying the same argument to $\sum|g_k|$ gives absolute convergence too. $\blacksquare$

blocks.question: Which choice of $M_k$ lets the M-test prove that $\sum_{k\ge1}\dfrac{x^k}{2^k}$ converges uniformly on $[-1,1]$?
blocks.explanation: On $[-1,1]$, $|x^k/2^k|\le\frac1{2^k}$ and $\sum\frac1{2^k}=1$ converges. $\frac{x^k}{2^k}$ depends on $x$, so it is not an M-test bound. $\frac1k$ and $1$ are valid bounds, but their series diverge, so the test gives no conclusion.

cards.back:
$f_n\to f$ with **one** $N$ for all $x$: $\forall\varepsilon\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N\ \forall x$, $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$.

*Example:* $\frac{\sin(nx)}{n}\to0$ uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$.

The worst gap $M_n=\sup_{x\in E}|f_n(x)-f(x)|$, also written $\|f_n-f\|_\infty$. Uniform convergence means **$M_n\to0$**.

*Example:* $x^n$ on $[0,\frac12]$ has $M_n=2^{-n}$.

Points $x_n$ (moving with $n$) where $|f_n(x_n)-f(x_n)|\ge\varepsilon_0$. They prove convergence is **not** uniform.

*Example:* $x_n=2^{-1/n}$ for $x^n$ on $[0,1)$.

$\forall\varepsilon\ \exists N$: $\sup_E|f_n-f_m|<\varepsilon$ for all $m,n\ge N$. Equivalent to uniform convergence, with **no limit needed**.

*Example:* partial sums of $\sum\frac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$.

If $|g_k(x)|\le M_k$ for all $x$, with constants $M_k$ and $\sum M_k<\infty$, then $\sum g_k$ converges **uniformly**.

*Example:* $\sum\frac{x^k}{k^2}$ on $[-1,1]$, $M_k=\frac1{k^2}$.

Every point converges, but the needed $N(x)$ is **unbounded**.

*Example:* $\frac{x}{n}\to0$ on $\mathbb{R}$, yet $f_n(n)=1$.

blocks.question: A sequence on $[0,1]$ has sup distance $M_n=\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|f_n(x)-f(x)|=\dfrac{1}{\ln(n+1)}$. What can you conclude?
options: The convergence is not uniform, because $M_n$ shrinks too slowly
Nothing, unless you also find witness points
blocks.explanation: $\frac1{\ln(n+1)}\to0$, slowly but surely, and $M_n\to0$ is exactly uniform convergence. The definition cares only that $M_n\to0$, not how fast. Witness points are for proving that convergence is **not** uniform, which would need $M_n\not\to0$.

blocks.prompt: Put the steps in order: **prove that $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+nx^2}$ converges uniformly to $0$ on $\mathbb{R}$, without calculus.**
items: For each fixed $x$, $f_n(x)\to0$, so the pointwise limit is $f=0$.
So $|f_n(x)|\le\dfrac{|x|}{2\sqrt n\,|x|}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt n}$ for every $x\ne0$, and $f_n(0)=0$.
Hence $M_n=\sup_{\mathbb{R}}|f_n|\le\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt n}\to0$, so the convergence is uniform. $\blacksquare$

blocks.title: Your turn: $\dfrac{nx}{1+n^2x^2}$
blocks.problem:
Let $f_n(x)=\dfrac{nx}{1+n^2x^2}$.

(a) Find the pointwise limit on $[0,1]$.
(b) Show the convergence is not uniform on $[0,1]$.
(c) Show it is uniform on $[a,1]$ for each fixed $a\in(0,1)$.

Try it before opening the solution.
blocks.solution:
**(a)** $f_n(0)=0$. For $x>0$, $0\le f_n(x)\le\dfrac{nx}{n^2x^2}=\dfrac{1}{nx}\to0$. So the limit is $f=0$.

**(b)** Look for a witness. The trouble is near $0$, and $nx=1$ at $x_n=\frac1n$:

$$f_n\Big(\frac1n\Big)=\frac{1}{1+1}=\frac12\quad\text{for every } n.$$

So $M_n\ge\frac12$ and $M_n\not\to0$: not uniform.

**(c)** For $x\in[a,1]$, the bound from (a) gives $0\le f_n(x)\le\dfrac{1}{nx}\le\dfrac{1}{na}$. This bound does not depend on $x$, so $M_n\le\frac{1}{na}\to0$: uniform. $\blacksquare$

**Check your version:** did you find the pointwise limit first? Is your witness point moving with $n$ (a fixed point cannot work)? In (c), is your bound free of $x$?

items.q: Is uniform convergence about converging fast?
items.a: No. It is about converging at the **same** rate everywhere. $M_n=\frac{1}{\ln(n+1)}$ is very slow but uniform. $x^n$ on $[0,1)$ is very fast at $x=0.1$ but not uniform, because of points near $1$.

items.q: Can the sup distance be infinite?
items.a: Yes. For $f_n(x)=\frac xn$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $|f_n(x)|$ is unbounded in $x$, so $M_n=\infty$ for every $n$. Then $M_n\not\to0$ and the convergence is not uniform, even though $\frac xn\to0$ at each point.

items.q: If I find a candidate $f$ and $M_n\to0$, do I need to check pointwise convergence separately?
items.a: No. $M_n\to0$ already forces $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ at every point. But if you guess the wrong $f$, $M_n$ simply won't tend to $0$, so finding the pointwise limit first saves effort.

items.q: Does the M-test tell me when convergence is not uniform?
items.a: No. It is a one-way test. If you cannot find summable bounds, the series might still converge uniformly; you then need another argument, such as estimating the tail or using witness points.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.md:
- **Uniform convergence:** one $N$, depending only on $\varepsilon$, works for every $x$. The quantifier $\forall x$ comes after $\exists N$.
- Test it with the **sup distance**: $f_n\to f$ uniformly exactly when $M_n=\sup_E|f_n-f|\to0$. Find the pointwise limit first.
- To disprove it, find **moving witness points** $x_n$ with gap at least a fixed $\varepsilon_0$.
- The same formula can converge uniformly on one set and not on another: $x^n$ on $[0,a]$ versus $[0,1)$; $\frac xn$ on $[0,1]$ versus $\mathbb{R}$.
- **Weierstrass M-test:** constant bounds $|g_k|\le M_k$ with $\sum M_k<\infty$ give uniform convergence of $\sum g_k$.

questions.prompt: Which sequence converges uniformly on $[0,1]$?
questions.explanation: $\sup_{[0,1]}|x/n|=1/n\to0$, so $\frac xn$ converges uniformly. For $x^n$ and $\frac{nx}{1+nx}$ the pointwise limit is discontinuous, and the sup distance stays near $1$. For $nxe^{-nx}$ the limit is $0$ but the value at the witness $x=1/n$ is $1/e$ for every $n$.

questions.prompt: If $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, then $f_n\to f$ pointwise on $E$.
questions.explanation: For each $x$, $|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le\sup_E|f_n-f|\to0$. The converse fails: $x^n\to0$ pointwise on $[0,1)$ but not uniformly.

questions.prompt: For $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1)$, what is $\sup_{x\in[0,1)}|f_n(x)-0|$ (the same for every $n$)?
questions.explanation: $x^n<1$ on $[0,1)$ but $x^n\to1$ as $x\to1^-$, so the supremum is $1$. Hence the convergence is not uniform.

questions.prompt: Let $f$ be the pointwise limit of $(f_n)$ on $E$. Which conditions are equivalent to $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$?
questions.explanation: The first two are the definition, and the fourth is the uniform Cauchy criterion (given that $f$ is the pointwise limit). The third is merely pointwise convergence.

questions.prompt: What does the Weierstrass M-test say about $\sum_{k\ge1}\dfrac{x^k}{k^2}$ on $[-1,1]$?
options: It converges pointwise but not uniformly
questions.explanation: $|x^k/k^2|\le1/k^2$ on $[-1,1]$ and $\sum1/k^2<\infty$. ($M_k=1/k$ would be a valid bound but $\sum1/k$ diverges, so the test would not apply.)

questions.prompt: If $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $A$ and uniformly on $B$, then $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $A\cup B$.
questions.explanation: $\sup_{A\cup B}|f_n-f|=\max\big(\sup_A|f_n-f|,\sup_B|f_n-f|\big)\to0$. (This fails for infinitely many sets: $x^n$ is uniform on each $[0,1-\frac1k]$ but not on their union $[0,1)$.)

questions.prompt: For $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{n}$ on $[0,5]$ and $\varepsilon=0.01$, what is the smallest $N$ such that $\sup_{x\in[0,5]}|f_n(x)|<\varepsilon$ for every $n\ge N$?
questions.explanation: $\sup_{[0,5]}|x/n|=\frac5n$, and $\frac5n<0.01$ exactly when $n>500$. So $N=501$. ($N=500$ gives $\frac{5}{500}=0.01$, which is not $<0.01$.)

questions.prompt: $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{n}$ converges uniformly to $0$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
questions.explanation: It converges pointwise, but $f_n(n)=1$ for every $n$, so $\sup_{\mathbb{R}}|f_n|\ge1$ (in fact it is $\infty$). On a bounded set like $[0,5]$ it is uniform.

questions.prompt: Which of these converge uniformly on the set given? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\sup|\sin(nx)/n|\le\frac1n\to0$ and $\sup_{[0,0.9]}x^n=0.9^n\to0$. $x^n$ on $[0,1)$ has sup $1$; $\frac xn$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has $f_n(n)=1$; $nxe^{-nx}$ equals $\frac1e$ at $x=\frac1n$.

questions.prompt: For $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+nx^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, what is $\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f_n(x)|$ when $n=4$? Give a fraction or decimal.
questions.explanation: The sup is $\frac{1}{2\sqrt n}$, attained at $x=\pm\frac1{\sqrt n}$. For $n=4$: $\frac{1}{2\cdot2}=\frac14$.

questions.prompt: In the Weierstrass M-test, the bounds $M_k$ are allowed to depend on $x$.
questions.explanation: The $M_k$ must be constants with $|g_k(x)|\le M_k$ for **every** $x$. That is what makes the tail estimate $\sum_{k>n}M_k$ the same for all $x$, which gives uniform convergence.

questions.prompt: To show $x^n$ does not converge uniformly on $[0,1)$ using $\varepsilon_0=\frac12$, which witness points give $x_n^n=\frac12$ exactly?
questions.explanation: $(2^{-1/n})^n=2^{-1}=\frac12$, and $2^{-1/n}<1$. The fixed point $\frac12$ gives $2^{-n}\to0$. $(1-\frac1n)^n\to\frac1e$, which also stays large but is not exactly $\frac12$. $x=1$ is not in $[0,1)$.

concepts.title: Uniform convergence and continuity
concepts.summary: The $\varepsilon/3$ argument: uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous.

blocks.title: Uniform convergence and continuity
blocks.md:
Pointwise limits of continuous functions can jump. Uniform limits cannot. This lesson proves that, and shows how to use it.

**In this lesson you will learn to:**
- state and prove that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (the $\varepsilon/3$ argument)
- use the theorem in reverse to show that a convergence is **not** uniform
- see that differentiability is **not** passed on to uniform limits, and what the correct theorem for derivatives says
- apply **Dini's theorem**, which turns pointwise convergence into uniform convergence under extra conditions

**You need:** continuity with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ (5.6), uniform convergence and the sup distance (8.9), metric spaces and the distance $d$ (8.1), compactness (8.4), and the triangle inequality (2.5).

## Why continuity can break in the limit

Each $f_n(x)=x^n$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, yet the pointwise limit is

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1,\end{cases}$$

which jumps at $x=1$. So pointwise convergence can destroy continuity.

The jump comes from **swapping two limits**. Compare the two orders at $x=1$:

- Let $n\to\infty$ first, then $x\to1^-$: for each $x<1$, $x^n\to0$, so $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1^-}\lim_{n\to\infty}x^n=\lim_{x\to1^-}0=0$.
- Let $x\to1^-$ first, then $n\to\infty$: for each $n$, $x^n\to1$, so $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\lim_{x\to1^-}x^n=\lim_{n\to\infty}1=1$.

The answers differ. Continuity of the limit $f$ at a point $x_0$ says exactly that the two orders agree:

$$\lim_{x\to x_0}\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\lim_{x\to x_0}f_n(x).$$

(The left side is $\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)$; the right side is $\lim_n f_n(x_0)=f(x_0)$ when each $f_n$ is continuous.) So the question "is the limit continuous?" is really "may we swap these limits?". The answer is yes when the convergence is uniform.

blocks.title: Continuous terms are not enough
blocks.md: "Every $f_n$ is continuous and $f_n\to f$" tells you nothing about the continuity of $f$ when the convergence is only pointwise. The examples $x^n$ on $[0,1]$ and $\frac{nx}{1+nx}$ on $[0,1]$ both have continuous terms and a limit with a jump.

blocks.question: For $f_n(x)=x^n$, what is $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1^-}\Big(\lim_{n\to\infty}x^n\Big)$?
blocks.explanation: For each fixed $x<1$, $x^n\to0$, so the inner limit is the constant $0$ on $[0,1)$, and its limit as $x\to1^-$ is $0$. The answer $1$ is what you get with the limits in the **other** order, $\lim_n\lim_{x\to1^-}x^n$. That the two orders differ is exactly why the limit function is discontinuous at $1$.

blocks.md:
## The theorem

**Plain words.** If, from some $n$ on, the graph of $f_n$ stays inside a thin band around the graph of $f$, then $f$ cannot jump. A jump of height $h$ in $f$ would force the continuous $f_n$, which has no jump, to be far from $f$ on one side of it once the band is thinner than about $h/3$.

**Theorem.** Let $(E,d)$ be a metric space (lesson 8.1) and $f_n,f:E\to\mathbb{R}$. If each $f_n$ is continuous at $x_0$ and $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $E$, then $f$ is continuous at $x_0$. In particular, **a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.**

**Examples.**
- $F(x)=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$. Each partial sum is a finite sum of continuous functions, and the M-test (lesson 8.9) with $M_k=\frac1{k^2}$ gives uniform convergence. You get continuity without ever finding a formula for $F$.
- $\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}\to|x|$ uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$ (shown below), and $|x|$ is indeed continuous.
- **Edge case:** the theorem is one-way. A continuous limit does not mean the convergence was uniform. $nxe^{-nx}\to0$ on $[0,1]$; the limit $0$ is continuous, but the value at $x=\frac1n$ is $\frac1e$ for every $n$, so the convergence is not uniform.
- **Edge case:** the domain need not be compact or bounded. The theorem works on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

blocks.question: Continuous functions $f_n$ on $[0,1]$ converge pointwise to a function $f$, and $f$ turns out to be continuous. What can you conclude about the convergence?
options: It may or may not be uniform
It is uniform, but only if $f=0$
blocks.explanation: The theorem only goes one way: uniform $\Rightarrow$ continuous limit. $\frac xn\to0$ on $[0,1]$ is uniform, while $nxe^{-nx}\to0$ on $[0,1]$ is not, and both have the continuous limit $0$. So a continuous limit settles nothing. (Dini's theorem, later in this lesson, adds conditions that do force uniformity.)

steps.title: State the goal
steps.md: Given $\varepsilon>0$, we must find $\delta>0$ with $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $d(x,x_0)<\delta$.

steps.title: Fix one $n$ using uniform convergence
steps.md: Choose $n$ with $\sup_{y\in E}|f_n(y)-f(y)|<\varepsilon/3$. The key point: this **one** $n$ works at every point, including $x_0$ and any $x$ we pick later. We fix $n$ now and never change it.

steps.title: Use continuity of this $f_n$
steps.md: Since $f_n$ is continuous at $x_0$, choose $\delta>0$ with $|f_n(x)-f_n(x_0)|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $d(x,x_0)<\delta$.

steps.title: Split three ways
steps.md:
For $d(x,x_0)<\delta$, add and subtract $f_n(x)$ and $f_n(x_0)$, then use the triangle inequality:

$$|f(x)-f(x_0)|\le\underbrace{|f(x)-f_n(x)|}_{<\varepsilon/3}+\underbrace{|f_n(x)-f_n(x_0)|}_{<\varepsilon/3}+\underbrace{|f_n(x_0)-f(x_0)|}_{<\varepsilon/3}<\varepsilon.$$

The first and third terms are small by the uniform choice of $n$, the middle one by the choice of $\delta$. $\blacksquare$

steps.title: See why pointwise fails
steps.md: With only pointwise convergence, the $n$ that makes $|f_n(x)-f(x)|$ small depends on $x$. But $\delta$ was chosen for a particular $f_n$, before $x$ is known. Changing $n$ after picking $x$ would change $\delta$ too, and the argument goes round in circles.

blocks.question: In the $\varepsilon/3$ proof, why must the chosen $n$ satisfy $\sup_{y\in E}|f_n(y)-f(y)|<\varepsilon/3$, rather than just $|f_n(x_0)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon/3$?
options: Because the same $n$ must also make $|f(x)-f_n(x)|$ small at every $x$ near $x_0$, and those $x$ are not known when $n$ is chosen
Because $f_n$ might not be continuous at $x_0$
It is not needed: closeness at $x_0$ alone is enough
blocks.explanation: The first term $|f(x)-f_n(x)|$ involves an arbitrary $x$ within $\delta$ of $x_0$. Since $n$ (and then $\delta$) is fixed before $x$, $n$ must work at all points at once, which is uniform convergence. Continuity of $f_n$ is a hypothesis, not the reason, and closeness at $x_0$ alone would leave the first term uncontrolled.

blocks.md:
## Using the theorem to rule out uniform convergence

Turn the theorem round (the contrapositive, lesson 1.10):

> If continuous $f_n$ converge pointwise to a **discontinuous** $f$, the convergence is **not** uniform.

This is often the quickest test. You only need the pointwise limit, with no sup to compute.

**Examples.**
- $x^n$ on $[0,1]$: the limit jumps at $1$, so not uniform.
- $\dfrac{x^n}{1+x^n}$ on $[0,\infty)$ (lesson 8.8): the limit is $0$ on $[0,1)$, $\frac12$ at $1$, and $1$ on $(1,\infty)$. Discontinuous, so not uniform.
- $\dfrac{nx}{1+nx}$ on $[0,1]$: worked out below.

**Edge case: the test only rules out.** On $[0,1)$, the limit of $x^n$ is the constant $0$, which is continuous. The test is silent, yet the convergence is still not uniform: the sup distance is $1$ for every $n$ (lesson 8.9). A continuous limit never proves uniform convergence; for that you still need $M_n\to0$ or a theorem like Dini's.

**Uniform away from the trouble.** The theorem only needs uniform convergence near the point in question. $x^n$ converges uniformly on each $[0,a]$ with $a<1$, so the limit is continuous at every point of $[0,1)$, which is true.

blocks.title: Worked example: using the theorem to rule out uniform convergence
blocks.problem: Show that $f_n(x)=\dfrac{nx}{1+nx}$ does not converge uniformly on $[0,1]$, but does converge uniformly on $[a,1]$ for each $a\in(0,1)$.
blocks.solution:
**Pointwise limit.** $f_n(0)=0$, and for $x>0$, $f_n(x)=\dfrac{1}{1/(nx)+1}\to1$. So the limit is $f(x)=0$ at $x=0$ and $f(x)=1$ for $0<x\le1$.

**Not uniform on $[0,1]$.** Each $f_n$ is continuous, but $f$ jumps at $0$. By the theorem, the convergence cannot be uniform.

**Uniform on $[a,1]$.** There $f=1$ and

$$|f_n(x)-1|=\frac{1}{1+nx}\le\frac{1}{1+na}\to0.$$

The bound does not depend on $x$, so the convergence is uniform on $[a,1]$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.prompt: Match each sequence to the right verdict.

pairs.right: Not uniform: the limit is discontinuous
Not uniform, although the limit is continuous: the sup distance is $1$
Uniform: the sup distance is at most $\frac1n$

blocks.title: Worked example: differentiability is not preserved
blocks.problem: Let $f_n(x)=\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Show $f_n\to|x|$ uniformly, although every $f_n$ is differentiable and $|x|$ is not.
blocks.solution:
Multiply and divide by $\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}+|x|$. For every $x$,

$$0\le\sqrt{x^2+\tfrac1n}-|x|=\frac{1/n}{\sqrt{x^2+1/n}+|x|}\le\frac{1/n}{\sqrt{1/n}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt n},$$

with equality at $x=0$. So $\sup_{\mathbb{R}}\big|f_n-|x|\big|=\frac1{\sqrt n}\to0$. Each $f_n$ is differentiable (smooth, in fact), but the uniform limit $|x|$ is not differentiable at $0$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.question: For $f_n(x)=\dfrac{\sin(n^2x)}{n}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, which statement is true?
options: $f_n$ does not converge uniformly, because the derivatives blow up
blocks.explanation: $\sup|f_n|\le\frac1n\to0$, so the convergence is uniform. But $f_n'(x)=n\cos(n^2x)$ and $f_n'(0)=n$. Large derivatives do not stop uniform convergence of the values, and uniform convergence of the values does not control the derivatives.

blocks.md:
## Dini's theorem: a partial converse

Sometimes you already know the limit is continuous and want uniform convergence for free. In general that fails ($nxe^{-nx}$), but it works under extra conditions.

**Plain words.** On a compact set, if continuous functions move **steadily in one direction** towards a continuous limit, they cannot linger behind at some moving point, so the convergence is uniform.

**Dini's theorem.** Suppose
1. $K$ is compact (lesson 8.4; for example a closed bounded interval),
2. each $f_n:K\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous,
3. $f_n\to f$ pointwise, with $f$ continuous, and
4. the sequence is monotone: $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ for all $n$, or $f_n\ge f_{n+1}$ for all $n$.

Then $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $K$.

**Examples.**
- $\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}$ on $[-1,1]$ decreases in $n$ to the continuous $|x|$. Dini gives uniform convergence, matching the direct calculation.
- $x^n$ on $[0,\frac12]$: decreasing, continuous, limit $0$, compact domain. Uniform.

**Non-examples, each missing one hypothesis.**
- $x^n$ on $[0,1]$: the limit is discontinuous.
- $x^n$ on $[0,1)$: not compact (the point $1$ is missing).
- $nxe^{-nx}$ on $[0,1]$: not monotone. At $x=\frac12$ the values are about $0.30$, $0.37$, $0.33$ for $n=1,2,3$: up, then down.

In each non-example the convergence really is not uniform, which shows that no hypothesis can be dropped.

blocks.question: Dini's theorem does not apply to $x^n$ on $[0,1)$, even though each $x^n$ is continuous, the sequence decreases, and the limit $0$ is continuous. Which hypothesis fails?
options: The pointwise limit is not continuous
blocks.explanation: $[0,1)$ is bounded but not closed, so it is not compact: the sequence $1-\frac1k$ in it has no subsequence converging to a point of $[0,1)$. The other three hypotheses hold, as the question says. And the convergence really is not uniform there, since the sup distance is $1$.

cards.back:
If continuous $f_n\to f$ **uniformly**, then $f$ is continuous.

*Example:* $\sum\frac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

Split $|f(x)-f(x_0)|$ into three pieces, each $<\varepsilon/3$: two by **uniform** convergence, one by continuity of a fixed $f_n$.

*Example:* the proof of the uniform limit theorem.

Continuous $f_n$ with a **discontinuous** pointwise limit cannot converge uniformly.

*Example:* $x^n$ on $[0,1]$.

Continuity of the limit means $\lim_{x\to x_0}\lim_n f_n(x)=\lim_n\lim_{x\to x_0}f_n(x)$. Uniform convergence **allows** the swap.

*Example:* for $x^n$ at $1$ the two orders give $0$ and $1$.

A uniform limit of differentiable functions **need not** be differentiable.

*Example:* $\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}\to|x|$ uniformly.

On a **compact** set, continuous $f_n$ converging **monotonically** to a continuous $f$ converge uniformly.

*Example:* $\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}\downarrow|x|$ on $[-1,1]$.

blocks.prompt: Put the steps in order: **prove that $F(x)=\sum_{k\ge1}\dfrac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.**
items: Each partial sum $S_n(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{\sin(kx)}{k^2}$ is a finite sum of continuous functions, so it is continuous.
By the Weierstrass M-test, $S_n\to F$ uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$.
A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so $F$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.title: Your turn: $\dfrac{1}{1+n^2x^2}$
blocks.problem:
Let $f_n(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+n^2x^2}$.

(a) Show that $(f_n)$ does not converge uniformly on $[-1,1]$.
(b) Use **Dini's theorem** to show that it converges uniformly on $[\frac12,1]$.

Try it before opening the solution.
blocks.solution:
**(a)** Pointwise limit: $f_n(0)=1$ for every $n$, and for $x\ne0$, $n^2x^2\to\infty$, so $f_n(x)\to0$. The limit is $1$ at $0$ and $0$ elsewhere, which is discontinuous at $0$. Each $f_n$ is continuous, so by the uniform limit theorem the convergence is not uniform on $[-1,1]$.

**(b)** Check the four hypotheses on $K=[\frac12,1]$:
1. $K$ is closed and bounded, so compact.
2. Each $f_n$ is continuous (the denominator is never $0$).
3. The limit on $K$ is the constant $0$, which is continuous.
4. For fixed $x$, $n^2x^2$ increases with $n$, so $f_n(x)$ decreases: $f_n\ge f_{n+1}$.

By Dini's theorem the convergence is uniform on $[\frac12,1]$. $\blacksquare$ (Directly: $0\le f_n(x)\le\frac{1}{1+n^2/4}\to0$.)

**Check your version:** in (a), did you name the theorem you used? In (b), did you check **all four** hypotheses, including that the limit is continuous on the new domain?

items.q: Does the theorem need uniform convergence on the whole domain?
items.a: No. Continuity is local, so uniform convergence on some neighbourhood of $x_0$ is enough for continuity at $x_0$. That is why the limit of $x^n$ is continuous at every point of $[0,1)$: the convergence is uniform on each $[0,a]$ with $a<1$.
Because the triangle inequality splits $|f(x)-f(x_0)|$ into **three** pieces. Any split adding up to at most $\varepsilon$ would do; thirds are just tidy.

items.q: If each $f_n$ is discontinuous, can the uniform limit be continuous?
items.a: Yes. $f_n=\frac1n\mathbf{1}_{[0,\frac12]}$ (equal to $\frac1n$ on $[0,\frac12]$ and $0$ elsewhere) jumps at $\frac12$, but $f_n\to0$ uniformly. The theorem says continuity is passed **on**; it says nothing about where continuity comes from.

items.q: I have seen "$C(K)$ is complete". What does that mean?
items.a: $C(K)$ is the set of continuous functions on a compact $K$, with distance $\sup_K|f-g|$. Completeness (lesson 8.6) says every uniformly Cauchy sequence in $C(K)$ converges uniformly to a function **in** $C(K)$. The limit exists by the uniform Cauchy criterion (8.9), and it is continuous by this lesson's theorem.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.md:
- A **uniform** limit of continuous functions is continuous. The proof is the $\varepsilon/3$ argument, with one $n$ fixed for all points.
- Contrapositive: continuous $f_n$ with a discontinuous pointwise limit do **not** converge uniformly.
- A continuous limit does **not** prove uniform convergence ($nxe^{-nx}$, $x^n$ on $[0,1)$).
- Differentiability is **not** preserved ($\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}\to|x|$); to differentiate a limit you need uniform convergence of the derivatives.
- **Dini:** compact domain + continuous $f_n$ + continuous limit + monotone in $n$ gives uniform convergence.

questions.prompt: If continuous functions $f_n:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ converge uniformly to $f$, then $f$ is continuous.
questions.explanation: This is the uniform limit theorem, proved by the $\varepsilon/3$ argument: fix one $n$ with $\sup|f_n-f|<\varepsilon/3$, use continuity of that $f_n$, and split $|f(x)-f(x_0)|$ into three pieces.

questions.prompt: Continuous $f_n$ on $[0,1]$ converge pointwise to a function $f$ that is discontinuous at one point. What can you conclude?
options: The convergence is not uniform on $[0,1]$
questions.explanation: A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so the convergence cannot be uniform. The $f_n$ are continuous by assumption, so "some $f_n$ must be discontinuous" contradicts the question. The limit may well be integrable (e.g. the limit of $x^n$).

questions.prompt: Which hypothesis of Dini's theorem fails for $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$?
questions.explanation: The pointwise limit is $0$ on $[0,1)$ and $1$ at $1$, which is not continuous. The other three hypotheses hold.

questions.prompt: Let $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$. Which properties of the $f_n$ are **guaranteed** to pass to $f$?
options: Riemann integrability (if every $f_n$ is Riemann integrable)
questions.explanation: Continuity, boundedness and Riemann integrability are preserved under uniform limits. Differentiability is not: $\sqrt{x^2+1/n}\to|x|$ uniformly.

questions.prompt: If each $f_n$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ and $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$, then $f$ is differentiable.
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{x^2+1/n}\to|x|$ uniformly, and $|x|$ is not differentiable at $0$.

questions.prompt: For $f_n(x)=\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}$, what is $\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\big|f_n(x)-|x|\big|$?
questions.explanation: $f_n(x)-|x|=\frac{1/n}{\sqrt{x^2+1/n}+|x|}$ is largest at $x=0$, where it equals $\sqrt{1/n}$.

questions.prompt: If $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[0,1]$ and $f$ is continuous, then each $f_n$ is continuous.
questions.explanation: Continuity passes from the $f_n$ to $f$, not back. For example $f_n=\frac1n\mathbf{1}_{[0,\frac12]}$ jumps at $\frac12$ for every $n$, yet $f_n\to0$ uniformly.

questions.prompt: A uniform limit on $\mathbb{R}$ of continuous functions $f_n:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, even though $\mathbb{R}$ is not compact.
questions.explanation: The $\varepsilon/3$ proof never uses compactness, only uniform convergence and continuity of each $f_n$. Compactness is needed for Dini's theorem, not for this one.

questions.prompt: Which inequality is the heart of the $\varepsilon/3$ argument?
questions.explanation: Adding and subtracting $f_n(x)$ and $f_n(x_0)$ splits the gap into two "uniform" terms and one "continuity" term. The second and third options are true but useless, and the fourth is not true in general.

questions.prompt: For $f_n(x)=\dfrac{\sin(n^2x)}{n}$, what is $f_n'(0)$ when $n=5$?
questions.explanation: $f_n'(x)=\frac{n^2\cos(n^2x)}{n}=n\cos(n^2x)$, so $f_5'(0)=5$. The derivatives at $0$ grow without bound even though $f_n\to0$ uniformly.

questions.prompt: Which hypotheses of Dini's theorem hold for $f_n(x)=nxe^{-nx}$ on $[0,1]$? Select all that apply.
options: The sequence $(f_n(x))$ is monotone in $n$ for every $x$
questions.explanation: $[0,1]$ is compact, each $f_n$ is continuous, and the limit is the constant $0$. Monotonicity fails: at $x=\frac12$ the values rise from about $0.30$ to $0.37$ and then fall. Since the convergence is not uniform (the value at $\frac1n$ is $\frac1e$), this shows the monotone hypothesis cannot be dropped.

questions.prompt: Continuous $f_n$ on $[0,1]$ decrease pointwise to a continuous limit $f$. What does Dini's theorem give?
options: Nothing, because the limit is continuous
questions.explanation: All four hypotheses hold: $[0,1]$ is compact, the $f_n$ and $f$ are continuous, and the sequence is monotone. So the convergence is uniform on the whole of $[0,1]$.

concepts.title: Uniform convergence and integration
concepts.summary: On $[a,b]$, uniform convergence lets you swap $\lim$ and $\int$.

blocks.title: Uniform convergence and integration
blocks.md:
When can you say "the integral of the limit is the limit of the integrals"? This lesson gives a clean answer on closed bounded intervals.

**In this lesson you will learn to:**
- prove that uniform convergence on $[a,b]$ lets you swap $\lim$ and $\int$
- use the key estimate $\left|\int_a^b f_n-\int_a^b f\right|\le(b-a)\sup_{[a,b]}|f_n-f|$
- integrate a uniformly convergent series term by term, for example to find a series for $\ln$
- explain why the result fails on unbounded intervals and for pointwise convergence

**You need:** the Riemann integral and its properties (7.5–7.8), integrability of continuous functions (7.6), the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (7.9), uniform convergence and the M-test (8.9), and the previous lesson (8.10).

## Why we want to swap limits and integrals

Many integrals are easiest to find by approximating the integrand. If $f_n\to f$, it is tempting to write

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx=\int_a^b\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)\,dx=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This swaps two limits (an integral is itself a limit of Riemann sums), and as lesson 8.10 showed, swapping limits needs a reason.

Here is a reminder of how badly it can go. We use the **indicator function** $\mathbf{1}_A$ of a set $A$: it equals $1$ on $A$ and $0$ off $A$. Let

$$f_n=n\,\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}\quad\text{on }[0,1],$$

a rectangle of height $n$ over the interval $(0,\frac1n)$. Its area is $n\cdot\frac1n=1$ for every $n$. But at each fixed $x$, $f_n(x)=0$ once $\frac1n\le x$ (and $f_n(0)=0$ always), so $f_n\to0$ pointwise. Thus

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1f_n=1\ne0=\int_0^1\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n.$$

The rectangles get taller and thinner, keeping their area while squeezing towards $x=0$. Pointwise convergence never sees this, because no single point stays inside the rectangle.

A second goal is integrating series. $\frac{1}{1-x}=\sum_{k\ge0}x^k$, and integrating both sides should give a series for $-\ln(1-x)$. That integrates an infinite sum term by term, which is also a swap of limits.

blocks.title: Pointwise convergence does not move integrals
blocks.md: Even if every $f_n$ and the limit $f$ are integrable, pointwise convergence does **not** give $\int f_n\to\int f$. Continuity doesn't rescue it either: continuous "tents" of height $n$ over $[0,\frac2n]$ have area $\frac12\cdot\frac2n\cdot n=1$ and converge pointwise to $0$.

blocks.question: Let $f_n=n\,\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}$ on $[0,1]$. What are $\int_0^1f_n$ and the pointwise limit $f$?
blocks.explanation: The integral is height times width, $n\cdot\frac1n=1$. At $x=0$ every $f_n$ is $0$ (the interval $(0,\frac1n)$ is open), and at $x>0$ the values are $0$ once $\frac1n\le x$. So $f=0$ everywhere, with no infinite value. $\frac1n$ is the width, not the area.

blocks.md:
## The theorem

**Plain words.** If $f_n$ stays within $\varepsilon$ of $f$ at **every** point of $[a,b]$, then the area under $f_n$ is within $\varepsilon\times(\text{length})$ of the area under $f$. As $\varepsilon\to0$ the areas agree.

**Theorem.** Let each $f_n$ be Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ and $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$. Then $f$ is Riemann integrable and

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

The engine is the **key estimate**

$$\left|\int_a^b f_n-\int_a^b f\right|\le(b-a)\,\sup_{[a,b]}|f_n-f|.$$

**Examples.**
- $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1e^{x/n}\,dx$: on $[0,1]$, $|e^{x/n}-1|\le e^{1/n}-1\to0$, so $e^{x/n}\to1$ uniformly, and the limit is $\int_0^11\,dx=1$.
- $\displaystyle\int_0^3\Big(x+\frac{\cos(nx)}{n}\Big)dx$: the integrand is within $\frac1n$ of $x$ everywhere, so the key estimate gives an error of at most $\frac3n$, and the limit is $\int_0^3x\,dx=\frac92$.
- **Edge case:** the theorem is sufficient, not necessary. $x^n\to f$ on $[0,1]$ is **not** uniform, yet $\int_0^1x^n=\frac1{n+1}\to0=\int_0^1f$, since $f$ is $0$ except at one point. The swap can hold without uniform convergence; the theorem just doesn't promise it.

blocks.question: What is $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1 e^{x/n}\,dx$?
blocks.explanation: On $[0,1]$, $|e^{x/n}-1|\le e^{1/n}-1\to0$, so $e^{x/n}\to1$ uniformly and the integrals tend to $\int_0^11\,dx=1$. $e-1=\int_0^1e^x\,dx$ is the integral for $n=1$, not the limit.

steps.title: Show the limit is integrable
steps.md: If every $f_n$ is continuous, the uniform limit $f$ is continuous (lesson 8.10), hence Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ (lesson 7.6). So $\int_a^bf$ makes sense. (The general case is in the questions at the end.)

steps.title: Write the difference as one integral
steps.md:
By linearity of the integral (lesson 7.8),

$$\int_a^bf_n-\int_a^bf=\int_a^b(f_n-f).$$

steps.title: Move the absolute value inside
steps.md:
The triangle inequality for integrals, $\left|\int g\right|\le\int|g|$ (lesson 7.8), gives

$$\left|\int_a^b(f_n-f)\right|\le\int_a^b|f_n-f|.$$

steps.title: Bound by the sup
steps.md:
Let $M_n=\sup_{[a,b]}|f_n-f|$. Since $|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le M_n$ at every $x$, monotonicity of the integral gives

$$\int_a^b|f_n-f|\le\int_a^bM_n\,dx=(b-a)M_n.$$

The constant $M_n$ is the same at every point. That is where uniformity is used.

steps.title: Let $n\to\infty$
steps.md: Uniform convergence means $M_n\to0$. Since $b-a$ is a fixed finite number, $(b-a)M_n\to0$, so $\int_a^bf_n\to\int_a^bf$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.question: In the last step of the proof, why does it matter that the interval $[a,b]$ is bounded?
options: Because $(b-a)M_n\to0$ needs $b-a$ to be a finite number; with infinite length the bound says nothing
Because continuous functions are only integrable on bounded intervals
Because uniform convergence is impossible on unbounded intervals
It doesn't matter; the proof works on $[0,\infty)$ too
blocks.explanation: The estimate is $(b-a)M_n$. If the length is infinite, "$\infty\times M_n$" gives no information even when $M_n\to0$. Uniform convergence on unbounded intervals is perfectly possible ($\frac{\sin(nx)}{n}$ on $\mathbb{R}$), and later in this lesson you will see the swap genuinely fail on $[0,\infty)$.

blocks.md:
## Integrating series term by term

A series of functions $\sum g_k$ is the limit of its partial sums $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^ng_k$. For a **finite** sum, linearity already gives $\int_a^bS_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\int_a^bg_k$. Apply the theorem to $S_n$:

**Term-by-term integration.** If each $g_k$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and $\sum g_k$ converges uniformly on $[a,b]$, then

$$\int_a^b\sum_{k=1}^\infty g_k=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\int_a^b g_k.$$

The usual way to get uniform convergence is the Weierstrass M-test (lesson 8.9).

**Power series.** A power series $\sum c_k(x-a)^k$ with radius of convergence $R$ (lesson 4.15) converges uniformly on every closed interval $[a-r,a+r]$ with $0<r<R$: the M-test applies with $M_k=|c_k|r^k$, which is summable because the series converges absolutely at distance $r<R$. So power series can be integrated term by term over any closed interval inside the open interval of convergence.

**Examples.**
- $\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{x^k}{k!}=e^x$ on $[0,1]$, with $M_k=\frac1{k!}$. So $\sum_{k\ge0}\int_0^1\frac{x^k}{k!}dx=\int_0^1e^x\,dx=e-1$.
- $\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\cos(kx)}{k^2}$ on $[0,\pi]$, with $M_k=\frac1{k^2}$. Each $\int_0^\pi\cos(kx)\,dx=\frac{\sin(k\pi)}{k}=0$, so the whole integral is $0$.
- **Non-example:** $\sum_{k\ge0}x^k$ over $[0,1]$ diverges at $x=1$, and is not uniform on $[0,1)$ either (lesson 8.9). You must stop at some $t<1$.

blocks.title: Worked example: a series for the logarithm
blocks.solution:
Fix $t\in[0,1)$. On $[0,t]$ the geometric series $\sum_{k\ge0}x^k$ converges uniformly to $\frac1{1-x}$ by the M-test with $M_k=t^k$, since $|x^k|\le t^k$ there and $\sum t^k<\infty$.

Each term is continuous, so we may integrate term by term over $[0,t]$:

$$\int_0^t\frac{dx}{1-x}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\int_0^t x^k\,dx=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{t^{k+1}}{k+1}.$$

By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus the left side is $\big[-\ln(1-x)\big]_0^t=-\ln(1-t)$. $\blacksquare$

For example $t=\frac12$ gives $\ln2=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(1/2)^{k+1}}{k+1}=\frac12+\frac18+\frac1{24}+\cdots$.

Notice that we fixed $t<1$ **first**, so the closed interval $[0,t]$ stays away from $1$ where the geometric series misbehaves.

blocks.question: For $|x|<1$, $\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kx^{2k}$, uniformly on $[0,t]$ for each $0\le t<1$. Integrating term by term over $[0,t]$ gives which series for $\arctan t$?
blocks.explanation: $\int_0^tx^{2k}\,dx=\frac{t^{2k+1}}{2k+1}$, and the sign $(-1)^k$ stays. The left side is $\int_0^t\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\arctan t$. The second option divides by $0$ at $k=0$, the third differentiates instead of integrating, and the fourth loses the signs (it is the series for a different function).

blocks.md:
## When the interval is unbounded

On an unbounded interval the key estimate becomes $\infty\times M_n$, which is useless, and the swap can really fail.

**The escaping mass.** Let $f_n=\frac1n\mathbf{1}_{[0,n]}$ on $[0,\infty)$: height $\frac1n$ over an interval of length $n$. Then

$$\sup_{[0,\infty)}|f_n|=\frac1n\to0,$$

so $f_n\to0$ **uniformly**. Yet

$$\int_0^\infty f_n=\frac1n\cdot n=1\quad\text{for all }n,\qquad\text{while}\qquad\int_0^\infty0=0.$$

The area does not disappear; it spreads out further and further to the right. (Integrals over $[0,\infty)$ are improper integrals, lesson 7.11.)

**Bounded pieces are fine.** On any $[0,c]$ the theorem works. For $n\ge c$, $f_n=\frac1n$ on all of $[0,c]$, so $\int_0^cf_n=\frac cn\to0$. The area is lost only "at infinity".

Compare the two failures in this lesson:
- tall thin spikes ($n\,\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}$): not uniform; area concentrates at a point;
- long low plateaus ($\frac1n\mathbf{1}_{[0,n]}$): uniform but on an unbounded set; area escapes to infinity.

Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem (lesson 8.16) handles both situations with one condition.

blocks.question: Let $f_n=\frac1n\mathbf{1}_{[0,n]}$. For $n\ge10$, what is $\displaystyle\int_0^{10}f_n$?
blocks.explanation: For $n\ge10$, $f_n=\frac1n$ on the whole of $[0,10]$, so the integral is $\frac1n\cdot10=\frac{10}n\to0$, matching $\int_0^{10}0=0$. On a bounded interval the theorem works. The value $1$ is the integral over all of $[0,\infty)$, where the mass escapes.

cards.back:
If integrable $f_n\to f$ **uniformly on $[a,b]$**, then $f$ is integrable and $\int_a^bf_n\to\int_a^bf$.

*Example:* $\int_0^1e^{x/n}\,dx\to1$.

$\left|\int_a^bf_n-\int_a^bf\right|\le(b-a)\sup_{[a,b]}|f_n-f|$. Needs **finite length**.

*Example:* sup gap $\frac1n$ on $[0,3]$ gives error at most $\frac3n$.

If $\sum g_k$ converges **uniformly** on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\sum g_k=\sum\int_a^bg_k$.

*Example:* integrating $\sum x^k$ over $[0,t]$ gives $-\ln(1-t)$.

Equals $1$ on the set $A$ and $0$ **off** $A$.

*Example:* $n\,\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}$ is a rectangle of height $n$ over $(0,\frac1n)$.

$n\,\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}\to0$ **pointwise**, but every integral over $[0,1]$ is $1$.

*Example:* shows pointwise convergence is not enough.

$\frac1n\mathbf{1}_{[0,n]}\to0$ **uniformly** on $[0,\infty)$, but every integral is $1$.

*Example:* shows the interval must be bounded.

blocks.question: You need $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\sin(kx)}{k^3}\,dx$ and want to integrate term by term. What justifies this?
options: The M-test with $M_k=\frac1{k^3}$ gives uniform convergence on $[0,1]$, and each term is continuous
The series converges at every point of $[0,1]$
Nothing: term-by-term integration is never allowed for infinite series
blocks.explanation: $\left|\frac{\sin(kx)}{k^3}\right|\le\frac1{k^3}$ and $\sum\frac1{k^3}<\infty$, so the convergence is uniform on $[0,1]$ and the theorem applies. Terms tending to $0$ does not even give convergence, and pointwise convergence is not enough to swap (the spike example). Term-by-term integration is allowed exactly under uniform convergence.

items: For each $x\in[0,2]$, $\dfrac{nx}{n+x}=\dfrac{x}{1+x/n}\to x$, so the pointwise limit is $f(x)=x$.
On $[0,2]$, $\dfrac{x^2}{n+x}\le\dfrac4n$, a bound free of $x$, so the convergence is uniform.
Each $f_n$ is continuous, so the theorem gives $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^2f_n=\int_0^2x\,dx=2$.

blocks.title: Your turn: $\displaystyle\lim\int_1^2\frac{nx}{1+nx^2}\,dx$
blocks.problem:
Let $f_n(x)=\dfrac{nx}{1+nx^2}$ on $[1,2]$.

(a) Find the pointwise limit $f$.
(b) Show $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[1,2]$.
(c) Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_1^2f_n(x)\,dx$.

Try it before opening the solution.
blocks.solution:
**(a)** Divide top and bottom by $n$: $f_n(x)=\dfrac{x}{1/n+x^2}\to\dfrac{x}{x^2}=\dfrac1x$.

**(b)** Compute the gap:

$$\frac1x-\frac{nx}{1+nx^2}=\frac{(1+nx^2)-nx^2}{x(1+nx^2)}=\frac{1}{x(1+nx^2)}.$$

On $[1,2]$ we have $x\ge1$, so this is at most $\frac{1}{1\cdot(1+n)}=\frac1{n+1}$. The bound is free of $x$, so $\sup_{[1,2]}|f_n-f|\le\frac1{n+1}\to0$: uniform.

**(c)** Each $f_n$ is continuous, the interval is bounded, and the convergence is uniform, so

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_1^2f_n=\int_1^2\frac{dx}{x}=\ln2.\ \blacksquare$$

**Check your version:** did you find $f$ before estimating the gap? Is your bound in (b) the same for every $x\in[1,2]$? In (c), did you say which hypotheses of the theorem hold?

items.q: Is uniform convergence necessary for the swap?
items.a: No, only sufficient. $x^n$ on $[0,1]$ is not uniform, yet $\int_0^1x^n=\frac1{n+1}\to0$, which is the integral of the limit. When the theorem doesn't apply you need another argument, such as computing the integrals directly.

items.q: What if the $f_n$ are integrable but not continuous? How do we know $f$ is integrable?
items.a: Use upper and lower sums (lesson 7.3). For any partition $P$, each upper sum of $f$ is within $(b-a)M_n$ of the matching upper sum of $f_n$, and the same for lower sums. So $U(f,P)-L(f,P)\le U(f_n,P)-L(f_n,P)+2(b-a)M_n$. Pick $n$ with $2(b-a)M_n<\frac\varepsilon2$, then $P$ with $U(f_n,P)-L(f_n,P)<\frac\varepsilon2$, and the $\varepsilon$-criterion (lesson 7.5) gives integrability.

items.q: Does uniform convergence also let me differentiate term by term?
items.a: No. Integration smooths things out, differentiation magnifies wiggles. $\frac{\sin(n^2x)}{n}\to0$ uniformly but its derivative at $0$ is $n$ (lesson 8.10). To differentiate term by term you need the **derivatives** to converge uniformly.

items.q: Why does integration behave better than differentiation here?
items.a: The key estimate bounds the change in the integral by (length) $\times$ (sup gap). There is no such bound for derivatives: a tiny change in values can hide a huge change in slope.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.md:
- On a closed bounded interval, **uniform** convergence of integrable $f_n$ gives an integrable limit and $\int_a^bf_n\to\int_a^bf$.
- The **key estimate**: $\left|\int_a^bf_n-\int_a^bf\right|\le(b-a)\sup_{[a,b]}|f_n-f|$.
- Uniformly convergent series (often via the M-test) can be **integrated term by term**; power series can be integrated over any closed interval inside the interval of convergence.
- **Pointwise** convergence is not enough (the spike $n\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}$), and an **unbounded** interval breaks the estimate (the plateau $\frac1n\mathbf{1}_{[0,n]}$).
- Uniform convergence is sufficient, not necessary: $\int_0^1x^n\to0$ anyway.

questions.prompt: Compute $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1\left(x^2+\frac{\sin(nx)}{n}\right)dx$ as an exact fraction.
questions.explanation: $\left|\frac{\sin(nx)}{n}\right|\le\frac1n$, so the integrand converges uniformly to $x^2$ on $[0,1]$, and $\int_0^1x^2\,dx=\frac13$.

questions.prompt: If Riemann integrable $f_n$ converge pointwise on $[0,1]$ to a Riemann integrable $f$, then $\int_0^1 f_n\to\int_0^1 f$.
questions.explanation: $f_n=n\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}$ converges pointwise to $0$, but $\int_0^1f_n=1$ for every $n$. The rectangles keep area $1$ while getting thinner, which pointwise convergence cannot see.

questions.prompt: $f_n=\frac1n\mathbf{1}_{[0,n]}$ converges uniformly to $0$ on $[0,\infty)$, yet $\int_0^\infty f_n=1$ for all $n$. Which hypothesis of the theorem fails?
options: The domain of integration is unbounded
The limit function is not integrable
questions.explanation: The theorem is for bounded intervals $[a,b]$; the estimate $(b-a)\sup|f_n-f|$ has $b-a=\infty$ here. The other options are false: each $f_n$ is integrable, the convergence is uniform ($\sup|f_n|=\frac1n$), and the limit $0$ is integrable.

questions.prompt: In which situations is $\int_a^b f_n\to\int_a^b f$ **guaranteed** on a bounded interval $[a,b]$?
options: Each $f_n$ is Riemann integrable and $f_n\to f$ uniformly
Each $f_n$ is integrable and $f_n\to f$ pointwise
The $f_n$ are partial sums of $\sum g_k$, with each $g_k$ continuous and the series converging uniformly to $f$
Each $f_n$ is continuous and $f_n\to f$ pointwise
questions.explanation: Uniform convergence (of the sequence, or of the series) is enough. Pointwise convergence is not, even for continuous functions: continuous tent functions of height $n$ on $[0,\frac2n]$ have integral $1$ and converge pointwise to $0$.

questions.prompt: Using $\sum_{k\ge0}x^k=\frac1{1-x}$ uniformly on $[0,\frac12]$, the sum $\displaystyle\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(1/2)^{k+1}}{k+1}$ equals
questions.explanation: Integrating term by term over $[0,\frac12]$ gives $\int_0^{1/2}\frac{dx}{1-x}=-\ln\frac12=\ln2$.

questions.prompt: For Riemann integrable $f_n,f$ on $[a,b]$, $\left|\int_a^b f_n-\int_a^b f\right|\le(b-a)\sup_{[a,b]}|f_n-f|$.
questions.explanation: Linearity, the triangle inequality for integrals and monotonicity give exactly this estimate.

questions.prompt: If $f_n\to f$ pointwise on $[0,1]$ and $\int_0^1 f_n\to\int_0^1 f$, then the convergence must be uniform.
questions.explanation: $x^n$ on $[0,1]$: $\int_0^1x^n=\frac1{n+1}\to0=\int_0^1f$, but the convergence is not uniform (the limit is discontinuous). Uniform convergence is sufficient for the swap, not necessary.

questions.prompt: Using term-by-term integration, what is $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{x^k}{k!}\,dx$?
questions.explanation: The series is $e^x$, uniformly on $[0,1]$ by the M-test with $M_k=\frac1{k!}$. So the integral is $\int_0^1e^x\,dx=e-1$. Term by term: $\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{1}{(k+1)!}=e-1$. The last option equals $e$.

questions.prompt: For which of these may you integrate term by term over the interval shown? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The first four pass the M-test with $M_k=\frac1{k^2}$, $\frac1{k!}$, $\frac1{k^2}$ and $\frac1{2^k}$, so they converge uniformly and each term is continuous. $\sum x^k$ diverges at $x=1$, so there is no sum to integrate over $[0,1]$.

questions.prompt: A power series with radius of convergence $R>0$ can be integrated term by term over $[-r,r]$ for any $0<r<R$.
questions.explanation: On $[-r,r]$ the M-test applies with $M_k=|c_k|r^k$, which is summable because the series converges absolutely at $r<R$. So the convergence is uniform there.

questions.prompt: Suppose $f_n\to f$ uniformly on $[0,3]$ with $\sup_{[0,3]}|f_n-f|=\frac1n$. What bound does the key estimate give for $\left|\int_0^3f_n-\int_0^3f\right|$?
questions.explanation: The bound is (length) $\times$ (sup gap) $=3\cdot\frac1n=\frac3n$. Forgetting the length gives $\frac1n$; dividing by it gives $\frac1{3n}$.

questions.prompt: For $f_n=n\,\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)}$ on $[0,1]$, what is $\int_0^1 f_n$ for $n=50$?
questions.explanation: A rectangle of height $50$ and width $\frac1{50}$ has area $1$. The integral is $1$ for every $n$, although $f_n\to0$ pointwise.

concepts.title: Equicontinuity
concepts.summary: Continuity with one $\delta$ shared by a whole family of functions.

blocks.title: Equicontinuity
blocks.md:
Continuity lets each function choose its own $\delta$. Equicontinuity asks a whole family of functions to share one.

**In this lesson you will learn to:**
- define equicontinuity at a point and uniform equicontinuity, and place them next to continuity and uniform continuity
- show a family is equicontinuous using a common Lipschitz constant or a common bound on derivatives
- show a family is **not** equicontinuous by finding nearby points where some member jumps
- tell equicontinuity apart from uniform boundedness, the two conditions in the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem (lesson 8.13)

**You need:** continuity with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ (5.6), uniform continuity and Lipschitz functions (5.11), the Heine–Cantor theorem (5.12), the Mean Value Theorem (6.7), metric spaces (8.1), and uniform convergence (8.9).

## Why a shared $\delta$ matters

The Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem (lesson 3.10) says every bounded sequence of numbers has a convergent subsequence. Is there a version for functions: does every bounded sequence of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ have a uniformly convergent subsequence?

No. Take $f_n(x)=\sin(nx)$. Every $f_n$ is continuous and $|f_n|\le1$, but the graphs oscillate faster and faster, and no subsequence settles down to a single continuous function uniformly. Being bounded is not enough. We also need to stop the functions from becoming ever steeper.

Recall the ladder for **one** function $f$:
- **continuous at $x_0$:** for each $\varepsilon$ there is a $\delta$, which may depend on $\varepsilon$ and $x_0$;
- **uniformly continuous:** $\delta$ depends only on $\varepsilon$, not on the point (lesson 5.11).

Now take a **family** $\mathcal{F}$ of functions, that is, a set of functions all defined on the same space. (The curly letter $\mathcal{F}$ is just a name for the set.) Each member has its own $\delta$. **Equicontinuity** asks that one $\delta$ work for every member of the family at once. "Equi" means "equal": the same continuity for all.

For $\sin(nx)$ this fails at $0$: $\sin(nx)$ climbs from $0$ to $1$ between $x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{2n}$, so a $\delta$ that keeps $\sin(nx)$ within $\frac12$ of $0$ must be smaller than $\frac{\pi}{2n}$. Those numbers shrink to $0$, so no single $\delta>0$ serves every $n$.

blocks.title: Every member continuous is not enough
blocks.md: "Each $f\in\mathcal{F}$ is continuous" means: for each $f$ there is a $\delta$. Equicontinuity means: there is a $\delta$ for all $f$. As in lesson 1.3, swapping "for each $f$, there is $\delta$" into "there is $\delta$ for all $f$" gives a much stronger statement. Each $\sin(nx)$ is even uniformly continuous on $[0,1]$, yet the family is not equicontinuous.

blocks.question: For $f_n(x)=\sin(nx)$ at $x_0=0$ with $\varepsilon=\frac12$: the point $x=\frac{\pi}{2n}$ gives $f_n(x)=1$. What does this show?
options: Any $\delta$ that works for $f_n$ must satisfy $\delta\le\frac{\pi}{2n}$, so no single $\delta>0$ works for every $n$
The family is equicontinuous at $0$, with $\delta=\frac{\pi}{2n}$
blocks.explanation: At $x=\frac{\pi}{2n}$ the gap $|f_n(x)-f_n(0)|=1\ge\frac12$, so a working $\delta$ for $f_n$ cannot exceed $\frac{\pi}{2n}$. Since these shrink to $0$, there is no common $\delta$. Each $f_n$ is continuous; the failure is only in sharing. And $\delta=\frac{\pi}{2n}$ depends on $n$, which is exactly what equicontinuity forbids.

blocks.md:
## Equicontinuity at a point

**Plain words.** Near $x_0$, no member of the family can move far from its value at $x_0$, and "near" means the same distance for every member.

**Definition.** Let $(K,d)$ be a metric space and $\mathcal{F}$ a family of functions $K\to\mathbb{R}$. Then $\mathcal{F}$ is **equicontinuous at $x_0$** if

$$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall f\in\mathcal{F}\ \forall x\in K:\ d(x,x_0)<\delta\implies|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon.$$

The quantifier $\forall f$ comes **after** $\exists\delta$, so $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$ and $x_0$, but not on $f$. The family is **equicontinuous** if this holds at every $x_0\in K$.

**Examples.**
- $\{\sin x+n:n\ge1\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Adding a constant does not change differences: $|(\sin x+n)-(\sin x_0+n)|=|\sin x-\sin x_0|\le|x-x_0|$. So $\delta=\varepsilon$ works for every member.
- **Edge case:** the constant functions $f_n(x)=n$. Every difference is $0$, so any $\delta$ works. The family is equicontinuous even though the values run off to infinity. Equicontinuity controls how much functions **change**, not how big they are.
- $\{x^n:n\ge1\}$ on $[0,1]$ at $x_0=\frac12$: equicontinuous (shown in the worked example below).

**Non-example.** $\{x^n:n\ge1\}$ at $x_0=1$: just to the left of $1$, $x^n$ drops towards $0$ for large $n$, however close $x$ is to $1$.

blocks.prompt: Match each statement to the property it defines.

pairs.left: Family $\mathcal{F}$: $\forall\varepsilon\ \exists\delta\ \forall f\in\mathcal{F}\ \forall x$ near a fixed $x_0$

blocks.title: Worked example: $\{x^n\}$ is not equicontinuous at $1$
blocks.problem: Show that $\mathcal{F}=\{x^n : n\ge1\}$ on $[0,1]$ is not equicontinuous at $x_0=1$, although it is equicontinuous at every $x_0\in[0,1)$.
blocks.solution:
**Failure at $1$.** Take $\varepsilon=\frac12$ and let $\delta>0$ be arbitrary (we may assume $\delta<1$). Put $y=1-\frac\delta2$, so $|y-1|<\delta$. Since $0<y<1$, $y^n\to0$, so for large $n$, $y^n<\frac12$ and

$$|1^n-y^n|=1-y^n>\tfrac12.$$

So no single $\delta$ works for all $n$.

**Equicontinuity at $x_0<1$.** Fix $b$ with $x_0<b<1$. On $[0,b]$, $|(x^n)'|=nx^{n-1}\le nb^{n-1}$, and $nb^{n-1}\to0$, so $L=\sup_n nb^{n-1}$ is finite. By the Mean Value Theorem, all $x^n$ are $L$-Lipschitz on $[0,b]$: $|x^n-y^n|\le L|x-y|$. Then $\delta=\min\big(b-x_0,\ \varepsilon/L\big)$ works at $x_0$ for every $n$. (The first part of the minimum keeps $x$ inside $[0,b]$, where the bound holds.) $\blacksquare$

blocks.question: At which points of $[0,1]$ is the family $\{x^n:n\ge1\}$ equicontinuous?
options: At every point of $[0,1)$, but not at $1$
Nowhere, because the pointwise limit is discontinuous
blocks.explanation: Away from $1$ the derivatives $nx^{n-1}$ are bounded by a common constant, so one $\delta$ serves all $n$. At $1$ the functions drop steeply just to the left, and no $\delta$ works for all $n$. The discontinuous limit only causes trouble at the jump point $1$, not everywhere.

blocks.md:
## Uniform equicontinuity and Lipschitz families

**Definition.** $\mathcal{F}$ is **uniformly equicontinuous** if one $\delta$ works for every member **and** every point:

$$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall f\in\mathcal{F}\ \forall x,y\in K:\ d(x,y)<\delta\implies|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon.$$

On a compact $K$, equicontinuity at every point already implies uniform equicontinuity, by the same argument as Heine–Cantor (lesson 5.12) for a single function.

**The main source: a common Lipschitz constant.** Recall from lesson 5.11 that $f$ is $L$-**Lipschitz** if $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\,d(x,y)$ for all $x,y$. If every member of $\mathcal{F}$ is $L$-Lipschitz with the **same** $L$, then $\delta=\varepsilon/L$ works for all of them: $d(x,y)<\varepsilon/L$ gives $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\,d(x,y)<\varepsilon$.

**Via derivatives.** On an interval, if every $f\in\mathcal{F}$ is differentiable with $|f'|\le L$ (same $L$), the Mean Value Theorem gives $|f(x)-f(y)|=|f'(\xi)|\,|x-y|\le L|x-y|$. So a common derivative bound gives uniform equicontinuity.

**Examples.**
- $\{\sin(x+c):c\in\mathbb{R}\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$: derivatives $\cos(x+c)$ are bounded by $1$, so $\delta=\varepsilon$ works, even on the non-compact $\mathbb{R}$.
- $\{x^n\}$ on $[0,\frac12]$: $|nx^{n-1}|\le\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}\le1$ for all $n$, so the family is $1$-Lipschitz there.
- **Non-example:** $\{nx:n\ge1\}$ on $[0,1]$. Member $n$ has slope $n$, so the best Lipschitz constants are $1,2,3,\dots$ with no common bound. For $\varepsilon=1$, member $n$ needs $\delta\le\frac1n$. Not equicontinuous at any point.

blocks.question: Is $\{x\mapsto\sin(x+c) : c\in\mathbb{R}\}$ uniformly equicontinuous on $\mathbb{R}$?
options: No, because the family is infinite
blocks.explanation: $|\sin(x+c)-\sin(y+c)|\le|x-y|$ for all $c$, so $\delta=\varepsilon$ works for the whole family on all of $\mathbb{R}$. Infinite families can be equicontinuous, and compactness is only needed to upgrade pointwise equicontinuity to uniform; here we have the uniform version directly.

blocks.title: Worked example: a Lipschitz family
blocks.problem: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of functions $f$ on $[0,1]$ that are continuously differentiable (that is, $f'$ exists and is continuous) with $f(0)=0$ and $|f'(x)|\le1$ for all $x$. Show $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly bounded and uniformly equicontinuous.
blocks.solution:
By the Mean Value Theorem, for $f\in\mathcal{F}$ and $x,y\in[0,1]$ there is $\xi$ between them with

$$|f(x)-f(y)|=|f'(\xi)|\,|x-y|\le|x-y|.$$

**Equicontinuity:** given $\varepsilon>0$ take $\delta=\varepsilon$; then $|x-y|<\delta$ gives $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$ for every $f\in\mathcal{F}$.

**Uniform boundedness** (meaning one bound for all members and all points; defined properly in the next section): with $y=0$, $|f(x)|=|f(x)-f(0)|\le|x|\le1$. $\blacksquare$

Notice the condition $f(0)=0$ was needed only for boundedness. Without it, the constants $f=n$ would belong to the family.

blocks.question: Every function in a family on $[0,1]$ is differentiable with $|f'(x)|\le4$. For $\varepsilon=0.2$, which $\delta$ works for every member at once?
options: It depends on which function you pick
blocks.explanation: A common derivative bound $4$ makes every member $4$-Lipschitz, so $\delta=\varepsilon/4=0.05$ works: $|x-y|<0.05$ gives $|f(x)-f(y)|\le4|x-y|<0.2$. $\delta=0.8=4\varepsilon$ multiplies instead of dividing, and $\delta=0.2$ fails for $f(x)=4x$. A common $\delta$ is exactly what the shared bound provides.

blocks.md:
## Boundedness, and two more sources

**Definitions.** A family $\mathcal{F}$ on $K$ is
- **uniformly bounded** if one number $M$ bounds every member at every point: $|f(x)|\le M$ for all $f\in\mathcal{F}$ and $x\in K$;
- **pointwise bounded** if at each $x$, the values $\{f(x):f\in\mathcal{F}\}$ are bounded, possibly with a bound that depends on $x$.

**Boundedness and equicontinuity are independent.**
- $\{\sin(nx)\}$: uniformly bounded by $1$, **not** equicontinuous.
- $\{f_n=n\}$: equicontinuous, **not** bounded.
- $\{x^n\}$ on $[0,\frac12]$: both.
- $\{nx\}$ on $[0,1]$: neither.

That is why the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem (lesson 8.13) needs both conditions to produce uniformly convergent subsequences.

**Finite families are always equicontinuous** on a compact set: each of $f_1,\dots,f_N$ is uniformly continuous by Heine–Cantor, with its own $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_N$, and $\delta=\min(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_N)$ is still positive. With infinitely many functions the "minimum" can be $0$, which is exactly what happens for $\sin(nx)$.

**Uniformly convergent sequences are equicontinuous.** If continuous $f_n\to f$ uniformly on a compact $K$, then $\{f_n\}$ is uniformly equicontinuous. The proof below handles the infinitely many late terms with one $\varepsilon/3$ argument and the finitely many early terms with a minimum.

cards.back:
One $\delta$, **the same for every $f\in\mathcal{F}$**, with $d(x,x_0)<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$.

*Example:* $\{x^n\}$ at $x_0=\frac12$.

One $\delta$ for **all members and all points**: $d(x,y)<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$.

*Example:* $\{\sin(x+c)\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $\delta=\varepsilon$.

One $M$ with $|f(x)|\le M$ for **every** $f\in\mathcal{F}$ and every $x$.

*Example:* $\{\sin(nx)\}$ with $M=1$. *Non-example:* $\{f_n=n\}$.

$|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\,d(x,y)$ for all $f\in\mathcal{F}$, same $L$. Gives uniform equicontinuity with **$\delta=\varepsilon/L$**.

*Example:* all $f$ with $|f'|\le3$, $\delta=\varepsilon/3$.

Any finite family of continuous functions on a compact set is uniformly equicontinuous: take the **minimum** of finitely many $\delta$'s.

*Example:* $\{x,x^2,x^3\}$ on $[0,1]$.

If continuous $f_n\to f$ **uniformly** on a compact $K$, then $\{f_n\}$ is uniformly equicontinuous.

*Example:* $\{\sqrt{x^2+\frac1n}\}$ on $[-1,1]$.

blocks.question: A sequence $(f_n)$ on $[0,1]$ has $f_n(0)=0$ and $|f_n'(x)|\le5$ for all $n$ and $x$. Which properties does the family $\{f_n\}$ have?
options: Uniformly bounded, but possibly not equicontinuous
blocks.explanation: The common derivative bound makes every $f_n$ $5$-Lipschitz, giving uniform equicontinuity with $\delta=\varepsilon/5$. With $y=0$: $|f_n(x)|=|f_n(x)-f_n(0)|\le5|x|\le5$. Without the condition $f_n(0)=0$ the family could be unbounded (add constants $n$), which is the trap in the second option.

blocks.title: Proof: a uniformly convergent sequence is uniformly equicontinuous

steps.title: Set up
steps.md: Let $f_n:K\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous, $K$ compact, and $f_n\to f$ uniformly. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. We need one $\delta$ that works for every $f_n$.

steps.title: Pin the late terms to one function
steps.md: Uniformly convergent sequences are uniformly Cauchy (lesson 8.9), so there is $N$ with $\sup_K|f_n-f_N|<\varepsilon/3$ for all $n\ge N$. All the infinitely many terms from $N$ on stay close to the **single** function $f_N$.

steps.title: Use uniform continuity of finitely many functions
steps.md: By Heine–Cantor, each of $f_1,\dots,f_N$ is uniformly continuous on $K$. Choose $\delta_k$ for $f_k$ with tolerance $\varepsilon/3$, and let $\delta=\min(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_N)>0$. A minimum of **finitely** many positive numbers is positive; that is why we split off the late terms first.

steps.title: Handle the early terms
steps.md: For $n\le N$ and $d(x,y)<\delta\le\delta_n$: $|f_n(x)-f_n(y)|<\varepsilon/3<\varepsilon$.

steps.title: Handle the late terms with $\varepsilon/3$
steps.md:
For $n\ge N$ and $d(x,y)<\delta\le\delta_N$:

$$|f_n(x)-f_n(y)|\le|f_n(x)-f_N(x)|+|f_N(x)-f_N(y)|+|f_N(y)-f_n(y)|<\tfrac\varepsilon3+\tfrac\varepsilon3+\tfrac\varepsilon3=\varepsilon.$$

So $\delta$ works for every $n$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.question: In this proof, why not simply take $\delta$ to be the infimum of the $\delta_n$ over **all** $n$?
options: Because the infimum of infinitely many positive numbers can be $0$, and $\delta=0$ is useless
Because the infimum might not exist
Because the $\delta_n$ are not real numbers
blocks.explanation: The $\delta_n$ are positive reals bounded below by $0$, so the infimum exists (lesson 2.10), but it can equal $0$, as with $\sin(nx)$ where $\delta_n\le\frac{\pi}{2n}$. That is why the proof uses a minimum over finitely many and treats the rest with the $\varepsilon/3$ trick.

blocks.prompt: Put the steps in order: **prove that $\{\sin(x+c):c\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is uniformly equicontinuous on $\mathbb{R}$.**
items: By the Mean Value Theorem, $\sin(x+c)-\sin(y+c)=\cos(\xi+c)(x-y)$ for some $\xi$ between $x$ and $y$.
So $|\sin(x+c)-\sin(y+c)|\le|x-y|<\varepsilon$. Since $\delta$ did not depend on $c$, the family is uniformly equicontinuous. $\blacksquare$

blocks.title: Your turn: $\{\sin(ax)\}$
blocks.problem:
Let $\mathcal{F}=\{f_a(x)=\sin(ax):0\le a\le3\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

(a) Show $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly equicontinuous and uniformly bounded.
(b) Explain why the larger family $\{\sin(ax):a\ge0\}$ is not equicontinuous at $0$.

Try it before opening the solution.
blocks.solution:
**(a)** $f_a'(x)=a\cos(ax)$, so $|f_a'(x)|\le a\le3$ for every member. By the Mean Value Theorem every $f_a$ is $3$-Lipschitz, so $\delta=\varepsilon/3$ works for the whole family: $|x-y|<\varepsilon/3$ gives $|f_a(x)-f_a(y)|\le3|x-y|<\varepsilon$. Also $|f_a(x)|=|\sin(ax)|\le1$, so the family is uniformly bounded by $1$.

**(b)** Take $\varepsilon=\frac12$. For any $\delta>0$, choose $a$ so large that $\frac{\pi}{2a}<\delta$. Then $x=\frac{\pi}{2a}$ is within $\delta$ of $0$, but $|f_a(x)-f_a(0)|=|\sin\frac\pi2-0|=1\ge\frac12$. So no $\delta$ works for every member. $\blacksquare$

**Check your version:** in (a), is your $\delta$ free of $a$? In (b), did you fix $\varepsilon$ first and then defeat **every** $\delta$, choosing $a$ after $\delta$?

items.q: Does equicontinuous just mean every function is continuous?
items.a: No, that is much weaker. Each $\sin(nx)$ is continuous, but the family $\{\sin(nx)\}$ is not equicontinuous on any interval: the functions oscillate faster and faster.
No: $\{\sin(nx)\}$ is bounded by $1$ but not equicontinuous.
No: the constant functions $f_n=n$ form an equicontinuous family (every $\delta$ works), but they are not bounded. That is why Arzelà–Ascoli needs both conditions.

items.q: Does an equicontinuous family need differentiable members?
items.a: No. Lipschitz bounds and derivative bounds are convenient sources, not requirements. For example $\{|x-c|:c\in\mathbb{R}\}$ has a corner in every member, yet each is $1$-Lipschitz, so the family is uniformly equicontinuous.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.md:
- **Equicontinuity:** one $\delta$ for every member of the family; $\forall f$ comes after $\exists\delta$. Uniform equicontinuity also makes $\delta$ independent of the point.
- Each member being continuous, even uniformly, is **not** enough: $\{\sin(nx)\}$.
- A **common Lipschitz constant** $L$ (or a common bound $|f'|\le L$) gives uniform equicontinuity with $\delta=\varepsilon/L$.
- Finite families and uniformly convergent sequences of continuous functions on a compact set are equicontinuous.
- Equicontinuity and uniform boundedness are **independent**; Arzelà–Ascoli (lesson 8.13) needs both.

questions.prompt: Which family is equicontinuous on $[0,1]$?
questions.explanation: $|(\sin x+n)-(\sin y+n)|=|\sin x-\sin y|\le|x-y|$, a common Lipschitz constant. The family $\{x^n\}$ fails at $1$; $\{\sin(nx)\}$ has slopes $n$ at $0$; and $\{nx\}$ has slope $n$ everywhere, so neither has a common $\delta$.

questions.prompt: The constant functions $f_n(x)=n$ on $[0,1]$ form an equicontinuous family.
questions.explanation: $|f_n(x)-f_n(y)|=0$ for all $x,y,n$, so any $\delta$ works. The family is equicontinuous but not bounded.

questions.prompt: Every uniformly bounded family of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ is equicontinuous.
questions.explanation: $\{\sin(nx)\}$ is bounded by $1$ but not equicontinuous at $0$: $\sin(n\cdot\frac{\pi}{2n})=1$ while $\frac{\pi}{2n}\to0$.

questions.prompt: Which conditions guarantee that a family $\mathcal{F}$ of functions on $[a,b]$ is equicontinuous?
options: All $f\in\mathcal{F}$ share a common Lipschitz constant
Every $f\in\mathcal{F}$ is differentiable with $|f'|\le M$, the same $M$ for all $f$
$\mathcal{F}$ is a finite set of continuous functions
questions.explanation: A common Lipschitz constant (directly, or via a common derivative bound and the Mean Value Theorem) works. A finite family works by taking the smallest of finitely many $\delta$'s from uniform continuity (Heine–Cantor). Mere continuity of each member is not enough: $\{\sin(nx)\}$.

questions.prompt: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{f : |f(x)-f(y)|\le3|x-y|\text{ for all }x,y\}$. Which choice of $\delta$ works for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $f\in\mathcal{F}$?
questions.explanation: If $|x-y|<\varepsilon/3$ then $|f(x)-f(y)|\le3|x-y|<\varepsilon$. The other choices fail for some $\varepsilon$ (e.g. $3\varepsilon$ always fails for $f(x)=3x$).

questions.prompt: Every member of a family on $[0,1]$ is differentiable with $|f'|\le5$. For $\varepsilon=0.1$, what is the largest $\delta$ that the bound $\delta=\varepsilon/L$ gives? Give a decimal.
questions.explanation: Each member is $5$-Lipschitz, so $\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{5}=\frac{0.1}{5}=0.02$.

questions.prompt: Any finite family of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ is uniformly equicontinuous.
questions.explanation: Each member is uniformly continuous by Heine–Cantor, and the minimum of finitely many positive $\delta$'s is still positive.

questions.prompt: If every function in a family on $[0,1]$ is uniformly continuous, then the family is equicontinuous.
questions.explanation: Each $\sin(nx)$ is uniformly continuous on $[0,1]$, but member $n$ needs $\delta\le\frac{\pi}{2n}$ at $0$ when $\varepsilon=\frac12$, so no common $\delta$ exists.

questions.prompt: Which of these families are uniformly bounded on $[0,1]$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $|\sin(nx)|\le1$ and $0\le x^n\le1$ on $[0,1]$. The constants $n$, the values $nx$ at $x=1$, and $\sin x+n$ all grow without bound. Note that $\{\sin x+n\}$ and $\{n\}$ are equicontinuous but not bounded.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the family $\{x^n:n\ge1\}$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$?
options: Uniformly equicontinuous, since every member is $1$-Lipschitz there
Not equicontinuous, since it fails at $1$
Not equicontinuous, since the family is infinite
questions.explanation: On $[0,\frac12]$, $|(x^n)'|=nx^{n-1}\le\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}\le1$, so every member is $1$-Lipschitz and $\delta=\varepsilon$ works. The trouble point $1$ is not in $[0,\frac12]$, and infinite families can be equicontinuous.

questions.prompt: In the definition of "$\mathcal{F}$ is equicontinuous at $x_0$", the number $\delta$ may depend on which of these?
questions.explanation: The definition reads $\forall\varepsilon\ \exists\delta\ \forall f\ \forall x$, at a fixed $x_0$. So $\delta$ is chosen after $\varepsilon$ and $x_0$ are known, but before $f$. Allowing $\delta$ to depend on $f$ would just say each member is continuous at $x_0$.
